Chapter 9: Meaning and Purpose—Building a Life Worth Living.
Beyond all the routines and doctor visits, there’s a bigger question that quietly lingers in the background. What actually makes life meaningful now? If you’re dealing with illness or a disability, you might know what it’s like to suddenly face that question, to revisit old dreams and come to terms with new realities. The search for purpose—it can feel urgent, and yet, sometimes, just out of reach.
Imagine this: a woman who once felt defined by her career suddenly couldn’t work anymore. Her days stretched out, empty, and she worried that maybe her best years were already behind her. But then, a friend invited her to volunteer at a local shelter, reading stories to children. At first, she doubted she could really make a difference. But the kids’ laughter, their endless curiosity, the way their eyes lit up—something inside her shifted. She realized that purpose wasn’t about a job title or a paycheck. It was about connection. About giving. About being truly present.
Most people don’t realize just how much meaning can come from the little things. A good conversation with a neighbor, diving into a creative project, or even a small act of kindness—these moments become anchors. They remind us that life still has value, even when everything else feels uncertain. Some folks find their purpose by getting involved in advocacy, sharing their stories to help others feel less alone. For others, it’s about nurturing relationships, exploring new hobbies, or simply learning to savor what’s right in front of them.
There’s another story I want to share. A man, learning to live with visual impairment, discovered a deep passion for music. He started teaching lessons to kids in his neighborhood, passing on his love for rhythm and melody. Sure, it was different from what he used to do, but it brought real joy—and a sense of accomplishment. It became clear that meaning isn’t lost when life changes. It just finds new forms.
Here’s something to remember: purpose isn’t some far-off destination. It’s a practice. It’s the choice to engage, to seek out moments of connection and joy, even on tough days. Most people find their sense of meaning grows when they stay open to new experiences, when they let themselves be changed by everything they’ve been through.
